title: Laute I: Vokale und Umlaute
summary: Long vs short vowels and the three umlauts ä/ö/ü — the sounds that change what a word means

blocks.title: Vowels come long and short
blocks.body: German vowels come in **short** and **long** versions, and the length can change the word. *Stadt* (city) has a short *a*; *Staat* (state) has a long one. The rough rule: a **doubled vowel** (*Staat*), a vowel **+ h** (*Ofen*), or a vowel in an **open syllable** is long; a vowel followed by a **double consonant** (*Stadt, offen*) is short.

blocks.title: Tap to hear the length difference

blocks.prompt: Which word has a LONG vowel?
blocks.explain: *Staat* — the doubled *aa* is long. *Stadt* (short) and *offen* (double consonant) are both short.

blocks.title: The three umlauts: ä ö ü
blocks.body: German's special vowels are **ä, ö, ü** — a vowel with two dots. They're not decoration; they're their **own sounds**, made by keeping your tongue where it is for *a/o/u* but rounding or fronting your lips. *ä* ≈ the *e* in "bed". *ö* ≈ say *e* with rounded lips. *ü* ≈ say *ee* with rounded lips. The umlaut also often signals a **plural**: *Apfel* → *Äpfel*.
blocks.callout: Can't type the dots? *ä = ae*, *ö = oe*, *ü = ue* — the app accepts both.

blocks.title: The umlaut often flips singular → plural

pairs.note: Same word, add the dots, and it's plural.

blocks.prompt: Listen and type what you hear.
Type the German for 'beautiful' (with the long ö).
blocks.hint: It's an o with two dots — round your lips.
blocks.explain: *schön* = beautiful. Without the umlaut, *schon* means "already" — the dots really matter.
